items.title_orig: Sonic Guild Is Changing What It Means to Be a Music Community
items.article_text:
Written by Selena Fragassi | 
  
  
    June 16, 2026 - 9:05 am

What do Mike McCready, Stone Gossard, Kirk Hammett, Matt Berninger, Dave Matthews, and members of the Head and the Heart all have in common? Beyond being wildly successful artists, all remember what it was like to be struggling musicians—and today, they are paying things forward as supporters and donors of Sonic Guild.

The nonprofit’s mission is to support independent musicians through grants that provide critical funding artists need to stick with their craft. Whether it’s for making albums, hitting the road, investing in merch, hiring publicity and management services, or any of the other myriad expenses DIY artists incur, the hope is that it will help lead to more sustainable careers, so we don’t miss out on the Pearl Jams of tomorrow.

“If music is important to us, we can’t just sit on the sidelines and watch what’s going to happen as the industry keeps changing,” says Sonic Guild CEO Ben London. “We’re investing in the future. If you’re not nurturing the next generation, then the well will go dry at some point.” To his point, some notable alumni of the program include Black Pumas, Die Spitz, Shakey Graves, and Thunderpussy, who have all gone on to national acclaim.

Sonic Guild was first established in 2013 by Austin music fans Matt Ott and Colin Kendrick who wanted to find a way to directly connect music lovers with artists in a show of support. At the time, streaming was getting its grip on the industry, and the duo wondered why indie musicians weren’t supported in the same ways as the symphony or ballet or other traditional art. So, they came up with their own patronage community.

Sonic Guild is built on a membership model where members pay monthly or yearly dues that entitle them to attend monthly showcases that highlight emerging talent from their own backyards and the ability to voice their choice for the grant recipients. The membership fees, along with the aforementioned donors and corporate sponsors like Tito’s Handmade Vodka, fuel the benefit programs, which include artist grants up to $20,000, touring grants up to $1,500, and producer grants up to $7,500.

London joined the organization in 2018, desiring to bring a chapter of the guild to his community in Seattle. He had seen what Ott and Kendrick had accomplished in Austin and was taken aback by the impact. To date, Sonic Guild has invested more than $7.3 million dollars in music in its three hubs, also including a third chapter in Denver (and the team is already looking at potential markets to expand to).

“It felt like they cracked the code, that they found a way to get money into musicians’ pockets where there weren’t strings attached,” London reflects of the Sonic Guild model. “It wasn’t like the indie record deal that I signed back in the ’90s where it was like, you’re going to give me $5,000 and then you’re going to own all the rights to my records for eternity.” Back in the day, London was a member of Alcohol Funnycar, a Seattle alt rock group signed to C/Z Records and then went on to BMG and Sony/Columbia. As such, he has seen firsthand the growing obstacles that have made it more difficult for artists to make a living today.

“It used to be you could press a thousand records, or a thousand CDs, and sell them off the stage or in the back of your car and make your money back. And that’s a lot harder now. Not to mention the cost of a gallon of gas, and yet somehow guarantees seem to be about the same for emerging artists that they’ve been for the last 25 or 30 years,” he laments. “But new problems require new solutions. And that’s what we’re really focusing on.”

In his time building up Sonic Guild in Seattle, London (who previously worked for an early iteration of the MoPOP museum and was an executive with the Grammys) has been able to tap into his deep network to help the chapter thrive.

An early supporter was Stone Gossard, who told SPIN, “I’ve spent much of my life on tour, so I understand the challenges musicians face on the road. As a label owner [of Loosegroove Records], I also know how hard it is for emerging artists to build momentum. It’s great to support organizations like Sonic Guild that are building new solutions to help artists navigate those challenges.”

Tomo Nakayama is one example of a Seattle artist who has benefitted from Sonic Guild. In 2020, he received an artist grant that provided the seed money to build a home studio that helped him create music that ended up on Netflix’s “House of Ninjas.” This year, Nakayama also received tour support money to organize shows in Japan, where he has a strong following.

items.title_orig: Gregg Deal Fights Fascism w/ Dead Pioneers' Wagon Burner
items.article_text:
Jason and Paul welcome Dead Pioneers' founder and vocalist Gregg Deal back to the show to discuss their new album Wagon Burner. Gregg discusses songwriting in the United States in 2026, educating versus entertaining and why it's not his responsibility for you to "get it". It's a great conversation fit for a commencement speech and anyone who wants to punch nazis. Wagon Burner is out June 26.
